abstract: Language models have outpaced our ability to evaluate them effectively, but for their future development it is essential to study the frontier of their capabilities. We find real-world software engineering to be a rich, sustainable, and challenging testbed for evaluating the next generation of language models. To this end, we introduce SWE-bench, an evaluation framework consisting of $2true294$ software engineering problems drawn from real GitHub issues and corresponding pull requests across $12$ popular Python repositories. Given a codebase along with a description of an issue to be resolved, a language model is tasked with editing the codebase to address the issue. Resolving issues in SWE-bench frequently requires understanding and coordinating changes across multiple functions, classes, and even files simultaneously, calling for models to interact with execution environments, process extremely long contexts and perform complex reasoning that goes far beyond traditional code generation tasks. Our evaluations show that both state-of-the-art proprietary models and our fine-tuned model SWE-Llama can resolve only the simplest issues. The best-performing model, Claude 2, is able to solve a mere $1.96$% of the issues. Advances on SWE-bench represent steps towards LMs that are more practical, intelligent, and autonomous.

sections.body: Language models are deployed in chatbots and coding assistants, but existing benchmarks are saturated and miss the frontier of their abilities. The authors introduce SWE-bench, which asks a model to edit a codebase so that it resolves a GitHub issue. The edit is checked by running the repository's testing framework. Compared with prior coding benchmarks such as HumanEval, the tasks span multiple files and require long context. The paper also releases SWE-bench-train for training, and fine-tuned SWE-Llama 7b and 13b models based on CodeLlama. Claude 2 resolves only 1.96% of issues with sparse retrieval.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Existing benchmarks are saturated, so the authors propose SWE-bench, which draws tasks from real GitHub issues.

sections.body: SWE-bench pairs issues from popular Python repositories with merged pull requests. Construction has three stages: scraping pull requests from 12 repositories, keeping merged pull requests that resolve an issue and change test files, and keeping instances with at least one fail-to-pass test that install and run without errors. Reference solutions average editing 1.7 files, 3.0 functions, and 32.8 lines. A Lite subset of 300 instances covers 11 of the 12 repositories. Evaluation applies the generated patch, runs the associated tests, and reports the percentage of instances resolved.
sections.heading: SWE-bench
sections.headline: SWE-bench pairs GitHub issues with merged pull requests and grades patches by running the repository's tests.

sections.body: Off-the-shelf CodeLlama variants often output placeholder responses or unrelated code on these tasks. The authors fine-tune the 7 billion- and 13 billion-parameter CodeLlama-Python models on issue-patch pairs collected from 37 additional repositories. These repositories are disjoint from the evaluation repositories to avoid data contamination. The prompt holds the instructions, the issue text, and the relevant code files, and the target is the gold patch. Only the attention sublayer is trained, using LoRA. Training sequences above a token limit are excluded, which reduces the effective training corpus. The authors describe the resulting models as repository editors that run on consumer hardware.
sections.heading: SWE-Llama: Fine-tuning CodeLlama for SWE-bench
sections.headline: Fine-tuning CodeLlama-Python on issue-patch pairs produces SWE-Llama, open models that edit repositories.

sections.body: Codebases are far larger than a model's context window, so each input must select files. The authors use sparse retrieval (BM25, Robertson et al., 2009), which fills each context limit with retrieved files, and an oracle setting that supplies the files edited by the reference patch. The authors call the oracle setting less realistic, since an engineer may not know in advance which files to change. For the 27k limit, BM25 retrieves a superset of the oracle files in approximately 40% of instances, and retrieves none of them in almost half of the instances. Models evaluated are ChatGPT-3.5, GPT-4, Claude 2, and SWE-Llama.
sections.heading: Experimental Setup
sections.headline: Each model gets context from sparse retrieval or from oracle files that the reference patch edits.

sections.body: Models struggle on these tasks. Claude 2 is the best performer at 1.96% resolved with sparse retrieval, and 4.8% in the oracle setting. Resolution falls as total context grows, which the authors attribute to models failing to localize the code that needs changing. Collapsing unedited context in the oracle setting raises GPT-4 from 1.3% to 3.4% and Claude 2 from 4.8% to 5.9%. Generating whole files instead of patches lowers Claude 2 to 2.2%. The finetuned SWE-Llama models perform poorly with retrieved context, which the authors attribute to a shift in context distribution. Model patches are shorter than gold patches and rarely edit more than one file.
sections.heading: Results
sections.headline: Claude 2 is the best model at 1.96% resolved, and resolution falls as the total context length grows.

sections.body: The authors argue that multi-domain task collections and web-interaction benchmarks often use tasks that are too simple or narrow to reveal actionable insights about model capability. HumanEval and its extensions mostly test self-contained functions or closed-form completion. Work on machine learning for software engineering covers commit generation, review, bug localization, testing, and program repair. The authors state that none of the existing datasets present code context at the scale of SWE-bench. SWE-bench keeps real repository context, multi-file patches, and long inputs, and it can be easily extended to new languages and repositories.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Earlier benchmarks use narrow tasks or single functions, which SWE-bench extends to multi-file repository edits.

sections.body: All task instances are in Python, and the authors hope to expand coverage to more languages and domains. The experiments establish simple baselines rather than agent-based or tool-augmented methods, and the authors encourage future work on those approaches. The authors also state that execution-based testing alone cannot guarantee reliable model generations, because model code can be less comprehensive, efficient, or readable than human-written solutions. The conclusion says SWE-bench mirrors open-source collaboration, and the authors hope it supports LMs that are more practical, intelligent, and autonomous.
sections.heading: Discussion
sections.headline: Limitations include Python-only tasks, simple baselines, and execution tests that miss readability and efficiency.

sections.body: All data is collected from public repositories whose licenses permit software use, with license details in Table 12. The collection does not gather information about GitHub users and uses only data available through the public API and website. The work involves no human subjects, crowdsourcing, or human task workers. The authors state that the popularity-based repository filter does not rely on discriminative or biased heuristics. The planned release includes the task instances, collection and evaluation infrastructure, experimental results, SWE-Llama training data, and model weights, with documentation and feedback channels. The authors state that SWE-bench does not put forth immediately harmful insights.
sections.heading: Ethics Statement
sections.headline: SWE-bench uses public repositories with licenses permitting software use, and involves no human subjects or GitHub user data.

sections.body: The authors uploaded anonymized source code as a zipped file, organized into directories for dataset collection, evaluation, open-source model inference, and SWE-Llama training. The source includes inline documentation, and the full set of 2294 task instances is included. Sections A.2 and A.4 give technical details for the collection pipeline and evaluation procedures. The authors plan a formal public release as an open-source repository that includes the collection framework. They expect the benchmark to be highly reproducible.
sections.heading: Reproducibility Statement
sections.headline: The source code, all 2294 task instances, and technical details for collection and evaluation are provided for reproduction.

sections.body: The appendix expands the main text in several parts. It gives benchmark details, including PR scraping, task instance construction, execution-based validation, and continuous updates. It describes the construction process, with Table 9 listing each task instance field, and how problem statements and codebases are handled through mirror repositories. It explains how patch and test files are split, how executable contexts are created per release version, and how the evaluation pipeline works. Dataset statistics appear as cumulative distribution plots, and qualitative case studies compare model patches with gold patches.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix covers construction, field definitions, execution-based validation, dataset statistics, and case studies of model patches.
